Session 48. ONE ticket, ONE new file, and it is a pure-primitive class -- the whole point is that this repo's harness can EXECUTE it, unlike the bridge's.

BACKGROUND YOU NEED. This work was attempted once in nt8-mcp-bridge (handover 5.72) and the run ended ESCALATED. Two things went wrong there and neither can happen here:
  * the patch read a property that does not exist and `[compile] ok` could not see it, because BridgeTests.csproj excludes the file being edited. HERE the build gate compiles everything and the class names no NT8 type at all, so a wrong name is a compile error in round 1.
  * the class was put in the bridge, where RiskGuardWindow -- the OTHER writer to the same config -- cannot reach it, because the submodule direction is bridge -> core. That is why the file belongs in THIS repo.

The fifteen acceptance assertions were written BY HAND FIRST and are RED at the 1776/15 baseline. They live in tests/RiskGuardAddOnTests.cs, which you may NOT edit.

READ THE TESTS BEFORE YOU WRITE ANYTHING. They pin the namespace (NinjaTrader.NinjaScript.AddOns), the type name (GuardConfigEdit), and the method name and shape: `public static string Refuse(string mode, double trailingDrawdown, int minShadowSessions)`, returning null when acceptable. They reach it by REFLECTION, so getting a name wrong does not fail the build -- it fails the test with no hint. Copy the names character for character.

ADD NO NEW PARAMETERS. Three, exactly as the tests call it.

DO NOT return a string containing three underscores from Refuse(). The tests use `___`-fenced sentinels to detect the class being absent, and a real return value shaped like one would make them read a refusal as a missing class.

tickets.title: P2-27 / P1-117: nothing validates a guard-config VALUE, on either of the two write paths
tickets.defect:
Two writers reach one `RiskConfig` and NEITHER validates what a value MEANS.

  * `/api/riskguard/config` POST, in nt8-mcp-bridge. `P1-80` stopped it persisting a file nothing ever read back. `P2-41` made it MERGE the partial body onto the live config instead of deserializing the body alone, which had been giving every omitted field its DEFAULT and silently resetting Mode, MinShadowSessions and every StopGuard value while replying "applied".
  * `RiskGuardWindow.OnSaveConfigClick`, in this repo -- the WPF dashboard's Save button. Thirteen bare `int.Parse`/`double.Parse` calls straight onto the live config object (P1-117).

What neither addressed: nothing looks at what the values MEAN. The merged RiskConfig goes straight to `SaveAndReloadConfig`, and `SaveAndReloadConfig` DOES NOT RUN PREFLIGHT. So a config that cannot pass preflight is written to RiskGuard/config.json and reloaded happily, and the guard comes up DISARMED at the next restart -- with nothing about the file looking wrong.

That is survivable while the only writer is a deliberate API call. It stops being survivable the moment the editable UI lands, because the entire point of that page is an operator changing limits quickly, and the failure is silent and delayed: the write says `applied`, the page re-renders the value it just sent, and the guard is not protecting anything after the next restart.

This ticket builds ONLY the shared validator. Wiring the two callers is separate work.
tickets.spec:
ONE NEW FILE: `addons/GuardConfigEdit.cs`, namespace `NinjaTrader.NinjaScript.AddOns`.

```csharp
public static class GuardConfigEdit
{
    public static string Refuse(string mode, double trailingDrawdown, int minShadowSessions)
}
```

Returns `null` when the config is acceptable, otherwise a single operator-readable sentence naming the FIELD that is wrong and what would have been accepted.

It must name NO NinjaTrader type and no RiskGuard type -- no Account, no Instrument, no RiskConfig, no config object of any kind. Primitives only. That is what lets the harness execute it and a mutation battery mutate it, and it is the pattern fourteen Bridge*.cs files already follow.

Rules, and the tests pin each one:
  * `mode` must be one of shadow / live / disabled, compared CASE-INSENSITIVELY. Anything else is refused, and the refusal must NAME all three valid ones.
  * A null or whitespace `mode` is ACCEPTED, not refused -- it means 'not being changed'. The endpoint takes PARTIAL bodies by design (that is P2-41's merge) and refusing an omitted field would make every partial write fail.
  * `trailingDrawdown` must be STRICTLY POSITIVE. Zero is refused and negative is refused.
  * `minShadowSessions` must not be negative. ZERO IS ACCEPTED -- zero is not negative, and a test pins it.
  * Anything else is ACCEPTED -- return null.

REFUSAL TEXT. Two substrings are asserted, case-insensitively:
  * the trailing-drawdown refusal contains `trailing`
  * the MinShadowSessions refusal contains `shadow session`
Write the sentences an operator would want beside a form input; those substrings fall out of any honest wording. Do not pad the string to satisfy a grep.

ORDER OF CHECKS IS NOT PINNED, but return on the FIRST problem -- one sentence, not a list. A caller renders this next to one input.
tickets.context:
WHY REFUSAL-SHAPED AND NOT CLAMPING. A clamp turns an operator's 0 into a 2500 they did not choose and did not see -- the limit they are then held to is not the one on their screen. Refusing is the only answer that leaves the operator's model of their own protection correct. This repo's whole `configured / evaluated / enforcing` family is four shipped defects that are all one thing: a surface stating protection that does not exist.

THE `<= 0` RULE IS NOT INVENTED. `GuardRules.cs:262` already evaluates `c.Config.PnLRules.TrailingDrawdown <= 0 ? Off("no trailing drawdown set")` -- the guard's own live predicate for 'this rule is not protecting you'. This promotes it from REPORTING to REFUSING. Matching it exactly is the point; a different threshold would mean the API accepts a value the guard then reports as off.

WHY THE REFUSAL MUST NAME THE FIELD. `P1-90`'s resolver refuses an unresolvable account by listing the 96 real ones, and that is the standard here. A UI renders this string next to an input; "invalid configuration" is not actionable in a form with a dozen of them.

WHY AN UNKNOWN MODE IS THE FIRST RULE. `P1-72` has REGRESSED TWICE on this codebase and it is always the same shape: a surface advertises or accepts a value that nothing implements. `enabled` is the obvious thing an operator types for `live`. And `P2-93` is the same defect one layer in: `pure` and `override_with_friction` passed preflight's enforcement gate and then acted on nothing, because `IsActingMode()` names only `live` -- an operator had to WAIT OUT five shadow sessions to reach a mode that enforces nothing. Both are in the tests.

SCOPE WARNING, AND IT IS THE SUBTLEST THING HERE. `TrailingDrawdown` = 0 means two OPPOSITE things in this codebase. On the GLOBAL `PnLRules` it means the rule is OFF, which is what this validator refuses. On an `AccountRiskProfile` it is a deliberate SENTINEL meaning 'derive it' -- `RiskGuardAddOn.cs:2409-2411` resolves it to 5% of cash value, else the global -- and it is the shipped DEFAULT on every profile. Say so in the file header, so the next caller does not feed a per-account value in here and get a refusal that is wrong. There is a third `TrailingDrawdown` on `RiskManagerAddOn` (default 2000) as well.

WHY A POSITIVE ASSERTION AND NOT ONLY REFUSALS. A validator that refuses EVERYTHING satisfies every negative test in the suite. `P3-30`'s audit shipped behind three positive-only acceptance tests and fired on correctly protected accounts. Six of the fifteen assertions here are ACCEPTANCE cases for exactly that reason -- read them as the specification of what must still get through, not as filler.

tickets.note_expect_green:
All fifteen were VERIFIED red at the 1776/15 baseline before this ticket was written -- expect_green is matched against the runner FAILURE LINES and means red-now-green-after.

Every assertion here is UNCONDITIONAL. That is deliberate and it is a lesson, not a style: the bridge version of this ticket was REFUSED by the loop because two of its listed assertions sat behind an `if (!Refused(reason)) return;` guard, so while the class did not exist they did not FAIL, they never RAN. Do not add a guarded assertion to a test-first gate.

Two assertions in the bridge version also passed VACUOUSLY on their first run: CallRefuse answers a `___CLASS_MISSING___` sentinel while the class is absent, which is non-empty, so a bare IsNullOrEmpty check was satisfied by the class being ABSENT. Here Refused(), Accepted() and Mentions() all reject the sentinel, and Accepted() insists on exactly null.
